issues.legal_issue: An interested private person may invoke the Supreme Court’s discretionary special-leave jurisdiction to challenge a High Court judgment of acquittal.
material_facts: The State did not challenge the acquittal of the principal accused.
The deceased’s father, an interested private person, brought the challenge to the High Court’s acquittal before the Supreme Court.
The challenge alleged that the acquittal had resulted in a serious miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The private person’s appeal was maintainable, and the Court could entertain it under Article 136.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers a plenary, discretionary power on the Supreme Court and does not restrict who may invoke its jurisdiction. The power is exercised according to settled judicial principles, and special leave is not granted as a matter of course. The Court relied on Durga Shankar Mehta v. Thakur Raghuraj Singh, Mohan Lal v. Ajit Singh, Arunachalam v. P.S.R. Sadhanantham, and P.S.R. Sadhanantham v. Arunachalam.

predicates.special_leave_challenge_to_high_court_ac: A person seeks special leave to challenge a High Court judgment of acquittal.
predicates.applicant_is_interested_private_person: The person bringing the challenge is a private individual with an interest in the case.
predicates.alleged_serious_miscarriage_of_justice: The challenge asserts that the acquittal has caused a serious miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When an interested private individual seeks special leave to challenge a High Court acquittal on the ground of serious miscarriage of justice, the challenge may be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court reversing a trial court’s decision must give clear reasons for its contrary conclusions, and those reasons cannot be supplied by later arguments.
material_facts: The High Court reversed the trial court’s convictions and acquitted the accused.
The High Court gave conclusions without adequately analyzing the evidence or clearly explaining its reasons.
The respondents argued that the High Court’s conclusions could be supported by arguments made later.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s unreasoned reversal could not be supported by later arguments and warranted reversal.
issues.legal_principle: When an appellate court expresses a view contrary to the trial court’s, it must clearly state its reasons; arguments are not substitutes for reasons. The Court applied this requirement as a settled principle of appellate adjudication.

predicates.criminal_appellate_review: An appellate court reviews a decision made in a criminal trial.
predicates.appellate_court_reverses_trial_court_dec: The appellate court reaches a result contrary to the trial court’s decision.
predicates.appellate_court_gives_no_clear_reasons: The appellate court does not clearly explain the reasons for reaching its contrary result.

issues.definition: In criminal appellate review, a reversal of the trial court without clear reasons is unsustainable.

issues.legal_issue: Credible eyewitness testimony is not displaced merely because medical evidence suggests an alternative possibility, and evidentiary discrepancies must be assessed cumulatively and in context.
material_facts: Witnesses testified to two gunshots, one of which fatally injured the deceased, but the High Court proceeded as if there had been only one shot.
The High Court discounted eyewitnesses based on assumptions about whether they could have reached the scene.
The time correction in the first report was explained as having been made before the report was handed to police, and no evidence established that it was made later.

The doctor who first examined the deceased explained that examination in inadequate lantern light could have caused an error about blackening; the post-mortem doctor did not observe blackening or tattooing.
The eyewitness account was assessed as credible, while the doctor’s hypothetical answers did not establish that the eyewitness account was false.
No ballistic report was produced.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s treatment of the evidence was erroneous; the eyewitness account was not undermined by the stated medical or other discrepancies, and the acquittal of the principal accused was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Credible and trustworthy eyewitness evidence requires careful independent assessment and is not conclusively displaced by medical opinion that points to alternative possibilities. Evidence is evaluated for inherent consistency and probability, consistency with other credible evidence and undisputed facts, and the witnesses’ credibility and capacity to observe. A reasonable doubt must be actual and substantial and arise from the evidence, not from speculation. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Krishna Gopal and Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab, the latter holding that the absence of a ballistic report does not make direct evidence improbable.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding asks an appellate court to review an acquittal.
predicates.eyewitness_account_is_credible: The eyewitness account is found credible and trustworthy after independent assessment.
predicates.apparent_discrepancies_are_explained_or_: The apparent inconsistencies relied on to doubt the account are explained by the evidence or lack evidentiary support.
predicates.medical_opinion_only_suggests_alternativ: The medical evidence suggests alternative possibilities but does not conclusively contradict the credible eyewitness account.

issues.definition: When an appeal against acquittal concerns credible eyewitness evidence and the apparent discrepancies are explained or unsupported, medical evidence that only suggests alternatives does not justify maintaining an acquittal based on those discrepancies.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal on a charge of joint criminal liability should not be disturbed where the trial court carefully assessed the evidence, extended the accused the benefit of doubt, and no error in that assessment is shown.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted three accused of the charge based on joint criminal liability after dealing with the evidence and extending them the benefit of doubt.
The High Court did not disturb those acquittals in the State’s appeal.
The appellants did not show why the trial court’s conclusions were fallacious or otherwise ought to be reversed.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals of the three accused on the joint-liability charge remained undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no basis to reverse the trial court’s evidence-based decision to extend the accused the benefit of doubt, particularly where the High Court had also left the acquittals undisturbed and no error in the conclusions was demonstrated.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal_for_joint_liabi: The proceeding challenges an acquittal on a charge that the accused shared responsibility for another person’s offence.
predicates.trial_court_carefully_assessed_evidence_: The trial court considered the evidence and acquitted the accused because it gave them the benefit of doubt.
predicates.no_error_in_acquittal_is_shown: The party seeking reversal does not demonstrate why the trial court’s acquittal was erroneous.

issues.definition: An acquittal on a joint-liability charge remains undisturbed when the trial court carefully assessed the evidence, gave the accused the benefit of doubt, and no error is shown.

issues.legal_issue: Accused who participated in mischief after making preparation to cause hurt were properly convicted of that offence.
material_facts: The accused arrived together at the site of a property dispute; one carried a gun and three carried lathis.
They began demolishing a wall, and the trial court convicted them of mischief after preparation to cause hurt.
The High Court acquitted the three accused whose convictions on that charge were challenged.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s acquittals on the mischief charge were reversed, and the trial court’s convictions of the accused were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 440 of the Indian Penal Code applies to mischief committed after preparation has been made for causing death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of these. The Court held that the accused were rightly convicted under that provision.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal_for_prepared_mi: The proceeding challenges an acquittal for mischief committed after preparation to cause harm.
predicates.accused_participated_in_demolition: The accused took part in demolishing or damaging property.
predicates.accused_were_armed_or_prepared_to_cause_: The accused were armed or otherwise had made preparation to cause hurt.

issues.definition: On an appeal against acquittal for prepared mischief, the trial court’s conviction should be restored when the accused participated in damaging property and were armed or prepared to cause hurt.

issues.legal_issue: A sentence imposed for mischief after preparation to cause hurt is not excessive where the circumstances do not warrant a different sentence.
material_facts: The trial court imposed a custodial sentence and a fine for the mischief offence.
The Supreme Court considered whether the sentence warranted alteration and found no basis to impose a different sentence.
issues.conclusion: The sentence imposed by the trial court was affirmed as not excessive.
issues.legal_principle: The Court concluded that the sentence was not excessive so as to warrant a different sentence.

predicates.sentence_review_in_criminal_appeal: A sentence is considered in the course of a criminal appeal.
predicates.sentence_is_not_shown_to_be_excessive: The circumstances do not show that the sentence is excessive or requires alteration.

issues.definition: When a sentence is reviewed in a criminal appeal and is not shown to be excessive, it is affirmed.
